doc:
Package sdb is the API surface handed to Go scripts. A script is a plain
Go file (package main) defining:

	func Run(s *sdb.S) error

It can query any configured connection, loop with parameters, push results
into the results view, and export in any supported format.

funcs.name: IsCanceled

types.name: Batch
types.doc:
Batch is the rows between two nodes of a fragment: columns and rows,
with helpers to find, add, drop and filter.

methods.name: AddCol
methods.sig: func (b *Batch) AddCol(name, dbType string, fill func(row int) any)
methods.doc:
AddCol appends a column, filled by calling fill for each row (nil fill
leaves every value NULL). dbType is the driver type name a sink's
CREATE TABLE should map, or "" for text. A column of that name already
there is replaced in place instead, so AddCol is also "set a whole
column".

methods.name: Clone
methods.doc:
Clone copies the batch: the column list and every row slice, so the
copy can be changed without the original seeing it. Values themselves
are shared ([]byte included), as a transform is not expected to edit a
value in place.

methods.name: Col
methods.doc:
Col is the index of the column called name, or -1. Names are matched
exactly first, then without regard to case, so "ID" finds "id" when
there is no "ID".

methods.name: DBTypes
methods.doc: DBTypes lists the columns' driver type names, in order ("" where unknown).

methods.name: Drop
methods.doc: Drop removes the named columns (unknown names are ignored).

methods.name: Filter
methods.doc: Filter keeps the rows keep says to, in order.

methods.name: Get
methods.sig: func (b *Batch) Get(row int, name string) any
methods.doc:
Get is row's value in the column called name; nil when there is no such
column or row.

methods.name: Keep
methods.doc:
Keep reduces the batch to the named columns, in the order given — a
select and a reorder in one. A name the batch does not have is ignored.

methods.name: Len
methods.doc: Len is the number of rows; 0 for a nil batch.

methods.name: Names
methods.doc: Names lists the column names, in order.

methods.name: Rename
methods.doc: Rename changes a column's name, reporting whether it was there.

methods.name: Result
Set
methods.sig: func (b *Batch) Set(row int, name string, v any) bool
methods.doc:
Set puts v in row's column called name, reporting whether there was
such a column and row.

types.name: Cfg
types.doc: Cfg is a node's settings, every value a string: sdb.Cfg{"conn": "prod"}.

methods.name: Bool
methods.doc:
Bool is the value of key as a boolean: true/false, yes/no, on/off,
1/0, in any case; unset or blank is false.

methods.name: Clone
methods.doc: Clone copies the config.

methods.name: Duration
methods.sig: func (c Config) Duration(key string, def time.Duration) (time.Duration, error)
methods.doc: Duration is the value of key as a duration ("30s"), or def when unset.

methods.name: Int
methods.sig: func (c Config) Int(key string, def int) (int, error)
methods.doc: Int is the value of key as an integer, or def when unset.

methods.name: Lines
methods.doc:
Lines is the value of key split into lines, each trimmed, blanks
dropped — for a field whose items may themselves contain commas (a
filter rule, an argument value).

methods.name: List
methods.doc:
List is the value of key split into items: on newlines and commas,
each trimmed, blanks dropped. "id, name" and "id\nname" read alike.

methods.name: Str
methods.sig: func (c Config) Str(key, def string) string
methods.doc: Str is the value of key, or def when unset or blank.

types.name: Col
types.doc: Col is one column of a Batch: its name and the source's type name.

types.name: CopyOpts
types.doc:
CopyOpts shapes s.Copy: destination name, a Where or a whole Query as the
source, a column subset, Create/Truncate of the destination, a per-row
Transform. The zero value copies the whole table into an existing table
of the same name. Set ProgressEvery to have the script output report the
running row count.

fields.name: To
fields.doc: To names the destination table; empty means the source table's name.

fields.name: Query
fields.doc:
Query, when set, is the source instead of a table: one statement that
returns rows, with Args as its parameters. To is then required.

A write with RETURNING is a source too — "DELETE FROM jobs WHERE done
RETURNING *" moves rows. From Postgres its change commits only after
the load has, so a copy that fails leaves the source as it was; the
other engines commit it as it runs. A write without RETURNING has no
rows to copy, and is refused before it runs. Within one Postgres
database, a load that needs the rows the Query changed (an archive
with a foreign key into them, the rows moved back where they came
from) would wait on that uncommitted change for good; it fails on a
lock timeout instead — 30s, unless the session already has one (see
loadOptions) — and the source keeps its rows.

fields.name: Args
fields.doc:
Args are bind parameters for Query or Where, in the source's
placeholder style ($1 Postgres/bytdb, ? MySQL/SQLite).

fields.name: Columns
fields.doc:
Columns limits the copy to these source columns, in this order. The
destination columns have the same names.

fields.name: Where
fields.doc: Where filters the source table's rows: "created_at >= $1".

fields.name: Create
fields.doc:
Create makes the destination table when it does not exist yet. A
Postgres-to-Postgres copy of a table reproduces the source's column
types, NOT NULLs and primary key from the catalog; any other pairing
maps each column to a broad type on the destination (integer, float,
numeric, boolean, date, timestamp, bytes, text). Defaults, indexes
other than the key, and constraints are not copied.

fields.name: Truncate
fields.doc:
Truncate empties the destination first, in the load's transaction:
if the copy fails, the old rows are still there. Within one Postgres
database it is a DELETE rather than a TRUNCATE, whose lock would
stall the copy's own read — so a table can be copied onto itself
with a Transform to rewrite it in place.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is rows per INSERT on non-Postgres destinations (see
WriteOptions.BatchSize).

fields.name: Transform
fields.doc:
Transform is called on every row before it is written, and may
change values in place or return a new row of the same length.
Returning a nil row skips it; returning an error stops the copy and
rolls the destination back. Into Postgres a value may also be a Go
slice (an array: []string into text[]), a map or struct (JSON), a
time.Duration (an interval), a pointer, or a driver.Valuer.

fields.name: Progress
fields.doc:
Progress, when set, is called every ProgressEvery rows (default
100000) with the running total.

types.name: CopyStats
types.doc: CopyStats reports a finished copy; its String() is a one-line summary.

fields.name: From
fields.doc: "conn:table" (or "conn:query")

fields.name: To
fields.doc: "conn:table"

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: rows loaded

fields.name: Skipped
fields.doc: rows a Transform dropped

fields.name: Direct
fields.doc:
Direct is true when the rows streamed Postgres to Postgres as COPY
text, never decoded into Go values.

types.name: Env
types.doc:
Env is what a Go node runs in: the session (S), the parameters, the
values earlier fragments published, and a logger.

fields.name: Params
fields.doc:
Params are the pipeline's parameters, defaults and overrides
resolved; Vars are the values earlier fragments published, keyed
"frag.<fragment>.<name>" ("frag.orders.rows"). Both are what ${…}
in a node's config was substituted from; a Go node reads them here.

fields.name: Cfg
fields.doc:
Cfg is the node's own settings, after ${…} substitution and with
its plugin's defaults filled in — what New was given. A built-in
reads its config once, in New; a user plugin file's funcs have no
New of their own, so they read it here (e.Cfg.Str("column", "")).

fields.name: Batch
fields.doc:
Batch is the fragment's batch size: how many rows a source yields
per Next, and so how many a transform sees per Apply.

fields.name: Pipeline
fields.doc: Pipeline, Fragment and Node name where the node is, for messages.

fields.name: Fragment
fields.doc: Pipeline, Fragment and Node name where the node is, for messages.

fields.name: Node
fields.doc: Pipeline, Fragment and Node name where the node is, for messages.

fields.name: SourceEngine
fields.doc:
SourceEngine is the fragment's source engine ("postgres", "mysql",
"sqlite", "bytdb"; "" when the rows did not come from a database),
set by the source's Open. A sink creating a table on the same engine
keeps the source's exact column types with it.

fields.name: Logf
fields.doc: Logf writes a line to the run's log, prefixed with the node.

methods.name: Stop
methods.doc:
Stop asks the fragment to stop pulling batches from the source once the
current batch has gone through — what rows.limit does on reaching its
count. The sinks still commit what they have: a stop is an early end,
not a failure.

methods.name: Where
methods.doc: Where names the node for messages: "orders/clean".

types.name: Field
types.doc:
Field is one setting of a plugin. It has a Name, a Type (what the
inspector draws), Doc, Default, Required and, for an enum, its values.

fields.name: Enum
fields.doc: the values a FieldEnum takes

types.name: FieldType
types.doc: FieldType is what a Field holds. It decides what the inspector draws.

methods.name: Batch
methods.doc: Batch sets the fragment's batch size.

methods.name: Func
methods.doc:
Func adds a Go value as a node: a Source, Transform, Sink or Action, or
a func of one of these shapes —

	func(e *Env) (*Batch, error)             a source: the next batch, nil at the end
	func(b *Batch) (*Batch, error)           a transform
	func(e *Env, b *Batch) (*Batch, error)   a transform with the Env
	func(e *Env, b *Batch) error             a sink (its rows are counted; nothing to commit)
	func(e *Env) error                       an action

Its id is the kind, numbered. A spec with a Func cannot be written to
JSON or exported as a script (the func has no text); it runs.

methods.name: Named
methods.sig: func (f *FragmentBuilder) Named(id, plugin string, cfg Config) string
methods.doc: Named is Node with the id chosen.

methods.name: NamedFunc
methods.sig: func (f *FragmentBuilder) NamedFunc(id string, fn any) string
methods.doc: NamedFunc is Func with the id chosen.

methods.name: Node
methods.sig: func (f *FragmentBuilder) Node(plugin string, cfg Config) string
methods.doc:
Node adds a node of plugin with cfg and returns its id, made from the
plugin's last word ("read", then "read2").

methods.name: OnError
methods.doc: OnError sets what the fragment's failure does: "stop" (default) or "continue".

methods.name: Then
methods.sig: func (f *FragmentBuilder) Then(plugin string, cfg Config) string
methods.doc:
Then is Node wired from the node added last — a linear fragment reads
as src, Then, Then.

methods.name: ThenFunc
methods.doc: ThenFunc is Func wired from the node added last.

methods.name: Wire
methods.doc: Wire connects the nodes in a chain: rows flow from each to the next.

types.name: FragmentStats
types.doc: FragmentStats and NodeStats are the parts of RunStats.

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: rows the sinks committed, or an action's rows affected

fields.name: Direct
fields.doc: ran as a direct Postgres COPY

methods.name: Elapsed
methods.doc: Elapsed is the fragment's wall time so far, or in all.

types.name: JobPipeline
types.doc:
JobPipeline is one pipeline of a job's run: its step id in the job and
its stats (Status, Fragments, Rows(), …). A step skipped because one
before it failed has status skipped.

types.name: JobRun
types.doc:
JobRun is a job's run as s.RunJob returns it: its id, its outcome, and
each pipeline's stats in the job's order.

fields.name: Status
fields.doc: succeeded, failed, canceled

types.name: JobRunner
types.doc: JobRunner runs a job for RunJob and waits for it. The host provides it.

types.name: Kind
types.doc:
Kind is what a plugin builds. It is one of KindSource, KindTransform,
KindSink or KindAction.

fields.name: In
fields.doc: rows handed to it

fields.name: Out
fields.doc: rows it handed on (a sink: rows it committed)

fields.name: Batches
fields.doc: Apply/Write calls

fields.name: Elapsed
fields.doc: time inside the node

types.name: Params
types.doc: Params are a run's parameter overrides: sdb.Params{"days": "7"}.

types.name: Paths
types.doc:
Paths are the directories a session resolves names in: a script's
(script.run), a pipeline's (RunPipelineNamed), a job's (RunJob) — and
where a job run there leaves its record. The host sets them.

types.name: Pipeline
types.doc:
Pipeline is a pipeline being built in Go (sdb.NewPipeline); Fragment
is one of its fragments being filled.

methods.name: Desc
methods.doc: Desc sets the description.

methods.name: Fragment
methods.doc: Fragment adds a fragment and returns it to fill.

methods.name: Param
methods.doc:
Param declares a parameter with its default ("" for none) and,
optionally, a line of doc.

methods.name: Spec
methods.doc:
Spec is the pipeline built so far. It is the builder's own: Run reads
it, and a later Fragment call extends it.

types.name: PipelineOpts
types.doc:
PipelineOpts shape a run: Params, a Log line sink, Progress, one
Fragment only, or PreviewRows for a preview that writes nothing.

fields.name: Params
fields.doc:
Params override the spec's parameter defaults. A name the spec does
not declare is an error; a declared parameter with no default and
no override is one too.

fields.name: Log
fields.doc:
Log receives each line of the run's log: the fragments starting and
ending, every node's Logf. Nil means the host's Print.

fields.name: Progress
fields.doc:
Progress, when set, is called with a fragment's counters so far — a
snapshot, safe to keep — when the fragment starts (status running,
its nodes listed with zero counts), after every batch, and once more
when it ends, with its final status (succeeded, failed, canceled, or
skipped: not run, by Fragment or in a preview). So a host sees every
fragment's state change through this one callback, and its counters
in between. A host that draws it coalesces the batches; the runner
does not throttle.

fields.name: Fragment
fields.doc:
Fragment, when set, runs only the fragment of that name; the others
are skipped. A value an earlier fragment would have published is
then unknown (pass it as a param, or run them all).

fields.name: PreviewRows
fields.doc:
PreviewRows > 0 makes the run a preview: the source stops after
that many rows, every sink is replaced by a preview sink (the rows
go to the results view, nothing is written), and actions are
skipped. The way to try a transform on real data.

fields.name: Run
fields.doc:
Run is the run's own values, ${run.<name>} in any node's config:
the host's run id, what triggered it, the job it is a step of (see
RunVars). "date" and "started" default to the run's start when the
host does not set them, so ${run.date} works in a script's
s.RunPipeline as it does under the jobs engine.

types.name: PipelineSpec
types.doc: PipelineSpec is a pipeline as data — what a pipeline file holds.

methods.name: Clone
methods.doc:
Clone copies the spec deeply enough that editing the copy's fragments,
nodes and configs leaves the original alone (Fn values are shared).

methods.name: Fragment
methods.doc: Fragment is the fragment called name.

methods.name: JSON
methods.doc:
JSON is the spec as the file holds it: two-space indented, one node per
line group, so a diff reads as the change it is.

types.name: Plan
types.doc:
Plan is an explained statement: its steps (Root, Nodes), what it cost or
took, and dbc's findings about it (Insights). See package explain.

fields.name: Conn
fields.doc: connection name it ran on

fields.name: Statement
fields.doc: the statement explained

fields.name: Command
fields.doc: the EXPLAIN actually sent, for the record

fields.name: Analyzed
fields.doc:
Analyzed: the statement was executed and every step carries measured
rows, loops and time. Measured: the statement was executed and timed
as a whole, on an engine that cannot time its steps (SQLite, bytdb) —
the root carries the total, the steps carry nothing.

fields.name: ResultRows
fields.doc: Measured: the rows the statement returned

fields.name: Notes
fields.doc:
Notes are facts about how the plan was obtained that a reader must
know to read it right ("ran inside a transaction that was rolled
back"). They are not findings about the plan; Insights are.

fields.name: Metric
fields.doc:
Metric is the best measure this plan has, which the views size bars
and flame blocks by unless the user picks another (see Metrics).

fields.name: Raw
fields.doc:
Raw is the engine's own output, verbatim — what "copy the plan"
copies, since that is what a DBA or a search engine recognizes.

methods.name: FileName
methods.doc:
FileName is the name a saved or downloaded rendering of the plan takes:
plan-<conn>-<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>.<ext>, or plan-<stamp>.<ext> with no
connection.

methods.name: Finalize
methods.doc:
Finalize numbers the steps, links parents, derives every computed field
and runs the insight rules. Parsers call it last; it is idempotent, so a
caller that edits a plan (the db layer adding table sizes) calls it again.

Time is the subtle part. Engines report a step's time as an average per
loop, INCLUSIVE of its children, so:

	TotalMs(n) = ActualMs(n) × Loops(n)        (÷ workers inside a Gather)
	SelfMs(n)  = TotalMs(n) − Σ TotalMs(child)  clamped at 0

The clamp matters: a Postgres InitPlan, a CTE referenced twice, or a
parallel child whose per-worker average does not add up can make the naive
difference negative, and a negative bar is worse than a slightly
generous one.

methods.name: Findings
methods.doc:
Findings counts the plan's critical and warning insights — the ones
worth acting on; info-level notes are not counted.

methods.name: HTML
methods.doc:
HTML renders the plan as a self-contained interactive page: a tidy-tree
graph of the steps with heat-colored cards and data-flow edges, a flame
(icicle) view, the insights with copyable fixes, and a detail panel for
the selected step. It references nothing on the network — no CDN, no web
font — so it opens the same from a temp file, an email attachment, or an
air-gapped machine.

The plan travels as the Document JSON (see JSON) inside a
<script type="application/json"> block, parsed by the page at load. That
keeps one source of truth for what a plan contains: the page reads the
same document `dbc explain -t json` prints, weights included, so its bars
and blocks are sized exactly as the terminal's.

methods.name: Headline
methods.doc:
Headline is the plan's one-line summary: engine, how it was obtained, the
totals, the size.

methods.name: JPEG
methods.doc:
JPEG renders the picture as a JPEG. Quality 90 keeps text edges clean;
the flat fills compress well enough that higher buys nothing visible.

methods.name: JSON
methods.doc: JSON renders the plan as an indented Document.

methods.name: Mermaid
methods.doc:
Mermaid renders the plan as a Mermaid flowchart — the form a plan takes in a GitHub or GitLab comment, a wiki page, or a Notion doc, which draw a ```mermaid block as a diagram without anyone installing anything. flowchart BT ┌───────────────┐ n0["Hash Join
…"] │ n0 Hash Join │ ← the root on top n1["Seq Scan · orders
…"] └───────▲───────┘ n1 -->|"36.7k rows"| n0 │ 36.7k rows ┌───────┴───────┐ │ n1 Seq Scan │ └───────────────┘ WHY BOTTOM-TO-TOP. Every other view draws the root on top and the data flowing up into it. In Mermaid an edge A --> B puts B after A in the flow's direction, so "BT" with child --> parent gives the same picture — root on top, arrows pointing the way the rows go — without the reversed arrowheads a TD chart would need. WHAT A NODE SAYS. The same lines the graph's cards carry: the operation and what it works on, the step's most telling detail, rows, and its share of the metric the plan is best measured by. Heat and findings become classDefs (see mermaidClass) so a renderer that draws colors shows where the time goes, and one that does not still has the words. ESCAPING. Labels are double-quoted, and inside one Mermaid reads its own entity codes: #quot; for a quote, and #; for anything else. A plan's text is the user's SQL — full of quotes, <, >, # and | — so every character Mermaid or its HTML labels could read as syntax is written as a code (see mermaidText). The result never breaks the chart, whatever the statement holds.

methods.name: Metrics
methods.doc: Metrics lists the measures this plan can be viewed by, best first.

methods.name: Node
methods.doc: Node returns the step with the given ID, or nil.

methods.name: Nodes
methods.doc:
Nodes returns every step in preorder — a parent before its children,
children in the order the engine listed them — so Nodes()[i].ID == i.

methods.name: PDF
methods.doc:
PDF renders the picture (see picture.go) as a one-page PDF, the page
sized to the picture so nothing is scaled or split: a wide plan makes a
wide page, which a viewer fits to its window and a printer to its paper.

WHY A RASTER INSIDE A PDF, NOT VECTOR PDF. A vector page would need the
text laid out a second time with PDF's own font machinery — embedding
and subsetting the Go fonts as CID fonts to reach beyond Latin-1 — to
draw the same picture the raster already is. At the 2× scale the picture
is drawn at, the page is sharp on screen and on paper; what it gives up
is selecting the text, and the statement and findings are one "copy as
text" away in every dbc view. So the PDF is a thin, dependency-free
wrapper, written by hand below, around the tested renderer.

The file, object by object:

	1 Catalog ─► 2 Pages ─► 3 Page ─┬─► 4 content stream: "q W 0 0 H 0 0 cm /Im0 Do Q"
	                                └─► 5 Image XObject (RGB, Flate + PNG "Up" predictor)
	6 Info (Title, Creator, CreationDate)
	xref table, trailer

The image is Flate-compressed after the PNG "Up" filter (each row stored
as its difference from the row above). The picture is mostly flat fills,
so most rows are all zeros after the filter and compress to almost
nothing; plain Flate on raw pixels is several times larger.

methods.name: PNG
methods.doc:
PNG renders the picture as a PNG: lossless, and for a picture of flat
fills and text usually smaller than the JPEG too.

methods.name: Picture
methods.doc: Picture draws the plan. See the top of this file for what is on it.

methods.name: ResolveAliases
methods.doc:
ResolveAliases fills in the table behind each step that names only an
alias, from the statement's FROM and JOIN clauses, then re-runs the rules
so their suggestions can name real tables.

methods.name: Share
methods.doc: Share is the step's Self as a fraction (0–1) of the whole plan's.

methods.name: Text
methods.doc:
Text renders the plan as an indented tree with a column of numbers and a
bar per step — the headless `dbc explain` output, the "copy plan as text"
clipboard payload, and what the assistant is shown.

	Hash Join · (o.user_id = u.id)             36,650 rows          8.4 ms  31% ███▏
	├─ Bitmap Heap Scan · orders o             50,000 rows          6.2 ms  23% ██▎
	│  └─ Bitmap Index Scan · orders_status    50,000 rows          0.9 ms   3% ▎
	└─ Hash                                    15,659 rows          2.3 ms   9% ▉

The bar and percentage are each step's OWN share (self time, self cost),
so they add up to 100% down the column and point straight at the step
that matters; the tree lines carry the nesting.

methods.name: WriteFile
methods.sig: func (p *Plan) WriteFile(dir, ext string, data []byte) (string, error)
methods.doc:
WriteFile saves one rendering of the plan (the page, a PDF, a JPEG, the
Mermaid source) into dir under the same what-and-when name WriteHTML
uses, with ext as its extension, and returns its path. 0600 for the
reason WriteHTML gives: every rendering quotes the statement.

methods.name: WriteHTML
methods.doc:
WriteHTML saves the interactive page into dir (created if need be) under a
name that says what and when — plan-<conn>-<yyyymmdd-hhmmss>.html — and
returns its path. The file is 0600: a plan quotes the statement and its
literals, which are the user's business, and dir is usually the shared
temp directory.

types.name: PlanText
types.doc:
PlanText shapes Plan.Text: width, the metric bars are sized by, color,
and whether the findings are appended.

fields.name: Width
fields.doc: total line width; 0 = 100

fields.name: Metric
fields.doc: "" = the plan's best

fields.name: Color
fields.doc: ANSI colors, for a terminal

fields.name: Insights
fields.doc: append the findings

types.name: Plugin
types.doc:
Plugin describes a kind of node. A plugin file in plugins_dir declares
one as var Plugin = sdb.Plugin{…} — Name ("mask.email"), Kind, Label,
Doc and Fields — beside plain funcs the Kind calls for (Apply for a
transform, Next for a source, Write for a sink, Run for an action); the
loader leaves New and Check to itself. Fields are the node's settings,
drawn as the inspector's form and read in the funcs as e.Cfg.

fields.name: Name
fields.doc: "sql.read": a family, a dot, a verb

fields.name: Kind
fields.doc: what New returns

fields.name: Label
fields.doc: a few words for the palette: "SQL query"

fields.name: Doc
fields.doc: a paragraph: what it does, what its fields mean

fields.name: New
fields.doc:
New builds a node from a config already validated and filled with
defaults. It returns a Source, Transform, Sink or Action by Kind.

fields.name: Check
fields.doc:
Check, when set, looks deeper at a config than Validate's field
rules can — a Go field compiled, a cron line parsed — and returns
problems as messages. It must not touch a database. A message that
starts "warning: " (or has it after its place: "code:3:1: warning:
…") is a warning; any other is an error, which keeps a run from
starting.

fields.name: File

methods.name: Defaults
methods.doc:
Defaults is cfg with every unset field's Default put in. The result is
what New receives, so a plugin reads its defaults from one place.

methods.name: Field
methods.doc: Field is the plugin's field called name.

methods.name: Validate
methods.doc:
Validate is what is wrong with cfg by the field declarations alone: a
required field blank, an int or bool that does not parse, an enum value
not offered, a key no field has. Each problem is one message naming the
field; none means New may be called (after Defaults).

types.name: Reader
types.doc:
Reader streams a query's rows: for rd.Next() { row := rd.Row() }, then
rd.Err(). Close it (defer rd.Close()) if you stop before the end.

methods.name: Abort
methods.doc:
Abort ends the read as a failed one, whatever state it is in: the rows
are closed and, on Postgres, the read's transaction is rolled back — so
a DELETE … RETURNING whose rows went nowhere (the load that was to take
them failed) keeps its rows. Close would commit a read that ran clean to
the end; a caller that knows the rows were lost calls this instead. A
no-op once the Reader is closed.

methods.name: Close
methods.doc:
Close releases the query's connection — on Postgres after ending the
read's transaction: COMMIT when the read went well (to the end, or
stopped early by the caller), ROLLBACK after a failure. It is safe to
call more than once, and a deferred Close after reading to the end costs
nothing.

methods.name: Columns
methods.doc: Columns returns the result's column names.

methods.name: Count
methods.doc: Count is the number of rows read so far.

methods.name: DBTypes
methods.doc:
DBTypes returns the driver's type name for each column, upper case
("INT4", "TEXT", "DATETIME"); empty where the driver does not say.

methods.name: Err
methods.doc: Err returns the error that stopped Next early, if any.

methods.name: Next
methods.doc:
Next advances to the next row, reporting false at the end or on an error
(see Err). The Reader closes itself when it runs out.

methods.name: Row
methods.doc: Row returns the current row. Each call to Next makes a new slice.

types.name: Result
types.doc: Result is the tabular result type scripts receive from Query.

fields.name: Conn
fields.doc: connection name the statement ran on

fields.name: Query
fields.doc: the statement text

fields.name: Columns
fields.doc: column names

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: display-ready values (NULL rendered as "NULL")

fields.name: Raw
fields.doc: typed values, used for JSON export

fields.name: Duration
fields.doc: wall time for the statement

fields.name: Truncated
fields.doc: true when the row limit was hit

fields.name: IsExec
fields.doc: true for non-query statements (INSERT/UPDATE/...)

fields.name: Affected
fields.doc: rows affected, when IsExec

fields.name: Transposed
fields.doc:
Transposed marks a result turned on its side (export.Transpose): each
row is one of the source's columns, its name in column 0, so the HTML
renderings draw that column as row headers rather than as data.

methods.name: RowCount
methods.doc: RowCount returns the number of data rows.

types.name: RunStats
types.doc:
RunStats is a pipeline's run: each fragment's status, rows and node
counters, and the outcome. Its String is a one-line summary.

fields.name: Preview
fields.doc: nothing was written (Options.PreviewRows)

methods.name: Rows
methods.doc: Rows is the rows every fragment committed, in all.

methods.name: String
methods.doc:
String is a one-line summary: "pipeline orders-nightly: 2 fragments,
48213 rows in 1.4s (succeeded)".

types.name: S
types.doc: S is the session handle passed to a script's Run function.

methods.name: Canceled
methods.doc: Canceled reports whether the user has stopped this run.

methods.name: Conns
methods.doc: Conns returns the configured connection names.

methods.name: Copy
methods.sig: func (s *S) Copy(src, dst, table string, opt CopyOpts) (CopyStats, error)
methods.doc:
Copy copies table from connection src into connection dst:

	st, err := s.Copy("prod", "local", "public.orders", sdb.CopyOpts{
		Create: true, Truncate: true, Where: "created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'",
	})
	s.Print("%s", st) // copied 48213 rows prod:public.orders → local:public.orders in 1.4s (direct COPY)

Postgres to Postgres without a Transform or Args streams COPY to COPY and
never decodes a row; every other pairing goes row by row. Either way the
destination is loaded in one transaction (with its Create and Truncate),
so a failed or stopped copy leaves it as it was.

methods.name: Ctx
methods.doc:
Ctx returns the session's context. Long-running scripts can select on
s.Ctx().Done() (or check s.Canceled()) to bail out early.

methods.name: DB
methods.doc:
DB exposes the raw *database/sql.DB for a connection — the escape hatch
for transactions, prepared statements, or anything else database/sql can do.

methods.name: Exec
methods.sig: func (s *S) Exec(conn, stmt string, args ...any) (int64, error)
methods.doc:
Exec runs a non-query statement and returns the rows affected. Its server
notices are printed as Query's are.

methods.name: Explain
methods.sig: func (s *S) Explain(conn, stmt string, analyze bool) (*Plan, error)
methods.doc:
Explain describes how conn's database runs stmt, as the TUI's Ctrl+X and
`dbc explain` do. analyze runs the statement to measure it: on Postgres a
write is analyzed inside a transaction that is rolled back; on the other
engines a write is explained but not run. It runs on its own session, not
one the script shares with Query.

	p, err := s.Explain("pg", "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42", true)
	s.Print("%s", p.Text(sdb.PlanText{Insights: true}))
	for _, in := range p.Insights { if in.Severity != "info" { … } }

methods.name: Export
methods.sig: func (s *S) Export(r *Result, format, path string) error
methods.doc:
Export renders a result in the named format (csv|tsv|markdown|html|json|text)
and writes it to path — or to the system clipboard when path is empty.

methods.name: LoadPipeline
methods.doc: LoadPipeline finds a pipeline the way RunPipelineNamed does and parses it.

methods.name: Paths
methods.doc: Paths is where the session resolves script and pipeline names.

methods.name: Print
methods.doc: Print writes a Printf-style message to the script output.

methods.name: Query
methods.sig: func (s *S) Query(conn, query string, args ...any) (*Result, error)
methods.doc:
Query runs a statement with parameters on the named connection and
returns the result set. Use the placeholder style of the target driver
($1 for postgres/bytdb, ? for mysql/sqlite).

Server notices the statement raises (Postgres RAISE NOTICE and its kin)
are written to the script output, as Print does, before Query returns —
whether or not the statement failed.

methods.name: Reader
methods.sig: func (s *S) Reader(conn, query string, args ...any) (*Reader, error)
methods.doc:
Reader runs query on conn and streams its rows. Use the placeholder style
of the connection's driver ($1 postgres/bytdb, ? mysql/sqlite).

methods.name: RunJob
methods.sig: func (s *S) RunJob(name string, params Params) (*JobRun, error)
methods.doc:
RunJob runs the job called name — a file in the jobs directory (.json
may be left off) or a built-in example — with params overriding its
own, and waits for it to end. Stop (Ctrl+K) cancels it as it does a
query. The run comes back however it ended; the error is non-nil when
it did not succeed.

methods.name: RunPipeline
methods.doc:
RunPipeline runs a pipeline built with NewPipeline. Every fragment runs
in order, each sink committing at its fragment's end; the stats come
back complete even on error. Stop (Ctrl+K) cancels the run as it does a
query.

methods.name: RunPipelineNamed
methods.sig: func (s *S) RunPipelineNamed(name string, opt PipelineOpts) (*RunStats, error)
methods.doc:
RunPipelineNamed runs a saved pipeline: a file path, a name in the
pipelines directory (.json optional), or a built-in example.

methods.name: RunPipelineSpec
methods.doc:
RunPipelineSpec runs a pipeline given as data (ParsePipeline, or a
literal).

methods.name: Show
methods.doc: Show pushes a result to the results view (TUI) or prints it (headless).

methods.name: Writer
methods.sig: func (s *S) Writer(conn, table string, cols []string, opt WriteOpts) (*Writer, error)
methods.doc:
Writer starts a load into table on conn; rows passed to Write line up
with cols. Nothing is visible to other sessions until Close commits.

types.name: Stats
types.doc:
Stats is a sink's or an action's report. It holds the rows loaded (or
affected), a note, and Vars for later fragments
(${frag.<fragment>.<name>}); a go.sink's Commit or a plugin's Run
returns one.

fields.name: Rows
fields.doc: rows loaded, or rows affected

fields.name: Skipped
fields.doc: rows dropped along the way, when the node counts them

fields.name: Direct
fields.doc: the fragment ran as a direct Postgres COPY (see run.go)

fields.name: Shown
fields.doc:
Shown marks a sink that showed its rows rather than wrote them (a
preview): its Rows count toward the fragment's only when no sink
wrote any, so a preview beside a load does not double the total.

fields.name: Vars
fields.doc:
Vars are values for later fragments: a sink publishes "rows"; an
sql.exec publishes "affected". They are read as
${frag.<fragment>.<name>}.

types.name: WriteOpts
types.doc:
WriteOpts shapes s.Writer: Setup statements and Truncate run first, in
the load's transaction; BatchSize tunes INSERT batching off Postgres.

fields.name: Setup
fields.doc:
Setup statements run first, inside the load's transaction — a CREATE
TABLE, an ALTER, a DELETE of the slice being reloaded. If the load
fails they are rolled back with it (except where the engine commits
DDL on its own: MySQL).

fields.name: Truncate
fields.doc:
Truncate empties the table after Setup and before the first row, in
the same transaction: a reload either replaces the old rows or leaves
them alone, never a half-empty table.

fields.name: BatchSize
fields.doc:
BatchSize is rows per INSERT statement on engines loaded by INSERT
(everything but Postgres). 0 means 500. It is lowered automatically so
one statement stays under the engines' bind-parameter limits.

fields.name: Upsert
fields.doc:
Upsert, when set, names the columns a row is matched on: a row whose
values in them match an existing row's replaces that row's other
columns, any other row is inserted, and when one load carries a key
twice the last row wins. The columns must be among the Writer's and
carry a unique constraint (a primary key, a unique index) on the
table; without one the server's own error says so. Postgres and
SQLite only — see upsertEngine.

types.name: Writer
types.doc:
Writer loads rows into one table in one transaction: w.Write(row) per
row, then w.Close() to commit. defer w.Abort() rolls back on any early
return; it is a no-op after Close.

methods.name: Abort
methods.doc:
Abort rolls the load back. It is a no-op after Close or a previous Abort,
so `defer w.Abort()` is the idiom that guarantees an early return or a
panic never leaves a transaction open.

methods.name: Close
methods.doc:
Close sends any buffered rows and commits, returning the rows loaded.
After a failed Write it rolls back instead and returns that failure.

methods.name: Columns
methods.doc: Columns returns the column list rows are written in.

methods.name: Count
methods.doc: Count is the number of rows accepted by Write so far.

methods.name: Write
methods.doc:
Write queues one row; its values line up with Columns. A failure aborts
the whole load, and every later Write or Close returns the same error.
